## A Ladder of Models, Not One Final Model {#sec-lay-ch19}

## A Concrete Picture

A map can show a continent, a city, a building, or the pipes inside one room.
The city map is not false because it omits plumbing. The plumbing drawing is not
better for planning a cross-country trip. Scale and detail should match the
question.

The proximal-distal project uses a model ladder for the same reason, but its
models form branches rather than one sequence of increasingly complete replicas.
A double pendulum isolates coupling. A two-hand model represents separate
contacts. A flexible shaft adds storage. A dynamic base adds back-reaction.
Spatial and anatomical models address other omissions; neither their detail nor
their software name establishes an independently verified result. Each model
must answer a declared question through observables it can actually represent.

![Model Families Meet Through a Declared Comparison Contract; More Detail Does Not Establish Human Validity.](figures/proximal_distal_companion/fig_companion_evidence_ladder.svg){#fig-lay-model-ladder width=98% fig-pos="H" fig-alt="Planar coupling, two-hand constraints, shaft deformation, moving base, spatial contact, and biological allocation connect to a shared comparison contract for available outputs, frames, states, inputs, and events. Human tests separately require qualified measurements and predictions."}

## How the Mechanism Works

The bottom rung should be analytically transparent. Exact equations, limiting
cases, and pointwise decompositions reveal why a mechanism appears. Higher rungs
ask whether it survives added realism. If the sign reverses or effect vanishes,
the model boundary becomes a scientific result rather than an embarrassment.

### Common Observables Are the Handrail

Coordinates differ across tiers. A planar wrist angle has no one-to-one match in
a spatial model with two wrists and a flexible shaft. Comparing raw coordinates
would confuse model architecture with mechanism.

Instead, specify a comparison map for each model $m$:

$$
\mathbf y_m=h_m(\mathbf x_m,\mathbf u_m,\boldsymbol\theta_m).
$$

Here $\mathbf x_m$ is the full state, $\mathbf u_m$ the declared input, and
$\boldsymbol\theta_m$ the model parameters. The common output $\mathbf y_m$ might
contain club motion, a wrench at a named reference point, interface power, work,
and closure residuals. Every component needs units, signs, frame, event window,
system boundary, and an uncertainty or numerical-error allowance. A planar
result is a projection with restrictions; storing it in a three-component array
does not add out-of-plane dynamics.

Use the intersection of available outputs. A single-wrist pendulum does not
measure two individual hand wrenches; a rigid club has no shaft strain state.
Mark an unsupported quantity **unavailable** or **not applicable**, with the
reason. A zero imposed by a model assumption is not an observed zero. A shared
record format ensures compatible labels, not common physics or equal trajectories.

The power comparison needs particular care when one branch deforms. At separate
contact ports, retain

$$
P_{\mathrm{ports}}=\sum_i
\left(\mathbf F_i\cdot\mathbf v_i+
\mathbf M_i\cdot\boldsymbol\omega_i\right).
$$

The moments here are local contact moments, paired with their work-conjugate
angular velocities; positive power enters the chosen system. Reduction to one
resultant wrench and one rigid-body twist
requires compatible rigid motion at all those ports. For a counterexample,
apply outward axial forces of 10 N at two ends moving apart, each with outward
velocity 0.2 m/s in the same inertial frame.
The resultant force and moment are zero, yet the input power is 4 W. A rigid
center-of-mass motion alone misses that deformation power. This connects the
system boundary in Chapter 2, power accounting in Chapter 5, and shaft storage
in Chapter 15; it does not violate reference-point invariance for a rigid body.

### Matching Outputs Does Not Match the State

Two full states can have the same comparison output. In a manufactured
two-mass spring example, initially set the observed mass's position and velocity
to zero. Let $q_1$ and $q_2$ be displacements from the two masses' equilibrium
positions along the same axis, with spring extension $z=q_2-q_1$ and force
$+kz$ on mass 1. With mass 1 kg and stiffness 100 N/m, an omitted extension of
$+0.01$ m or $-0.01$ m gives that mass acceleration $+1$ or $-1$ m/s$^2$.
The reduced snapshot is identical; the stored elastic state is not. Activation,
contact history, and modal velocities can create analogous ambiguities.

Therefore register how a reduced initial condition is lifted into each full
state, including preload and stored energy, and whether the lift is unique.
Holding the same motion while reconstructing required loads is an inverse
comparison. Applying matched input histories or matched feedback policies and
letting motion evolve is a forward comparison. Deleting a command at one state
does not erase its earlier impulse or reproduce the trajectory obtained by
removing it throughout the swing. Chapters 3 and 11 supply those distinctions.

### Complexity Must Pay Rent

Adding states can expose uncertain parameters and alternative explanations, but
does not necessarily increase every uncertainty or destroy identifiability.
Known parameters, informative measurements, or a justified constraint can make
a richer model more predictive. Conversely, a smaller model can be precise
about the wrong quantity because it excludes important physics. Distinguish
approximation bias, numerical error, parameter uncertainty, and ambiguity in the
unobserved internal variables. A full-body animation does not resolve any of
these by itself.

The distributed shaft earns its extra states when omitted modes affect the
target beyond the declared tolerance, or when shaft behavior is itself the
target. A moving base matters when prescribed support hides relevant work or
back-reaction. Spatial contact matters when out-of-plane geometry or wrench
components matter. Compare predictions on data or conditions not used to tune
the model; improved training fit alone does not establish the improvement.

### Surviving and Changing Claims

Some statements are structural within their stated mechanics. Consistent
action-reaction, wrench transformation, and complete work-energy accounting
should survive a change of representation. Closure must include moving-support
work, storage, dissipation, and numerical residuals where relevant; zero energy
change is not the universal test. Some statements are model-specific: the
exact duration of a negative couple, optimal torque onset, or numerical force
magnitude can change with parameters and degrees of freedom.

The release matrix labels what each tier supports, omits, and must not claim.
This prevents a result from climbing the ladder merely because a later model
exists elsewhere in the repository.

### Cross-Formulation Agreement

Inverse, forward, reduced, and spatial formulations can share a common state or
observable. Agreement under independently implemented equations reduces the
chance that one code path created the effect. Disagreement helps locate hidden
assumptions.

The reviewed upstream release makes a narrower distinction than “two engines
agree.” Its nonplanar common-state inverse comparison uses MuJoCo and a separate
Lagrange--Christoffel formulation with prescribed hand loads. Its reduced spatial
forward-contact comparison uses native MuJoCo and Pinocchio inertia-and-bias
operators, but a **shared contact law and integrator**: projected compliant
contacts and the same semi-implicit update. That checks transport through those
rigid-body operators; it is not agreement between independently authored native
contact solvers or integration schemes. The separate native-formulation control
reports a discrepancy rather than proving their equivalence.

Report which equations, code, calibration, contact law, and time integration are
independent. Compare the physical generalized reaction or a declared contact wrench,
not raw redundant multipliers whose values depend on constraint coordinates
(Chapter 6). Check converged observables and residuals under refinement, with
event alignment stated. Identical bugs in a shared layer can survive perfect
cross-engine agreement. Pinocchio is a rigid-body dynamics library; using it in
a simulation does not imply that it independently supplied every component of
that simulation.

### The Ladder Ends at an Open Gate

No computational branch becomes a human trial. Select measurements from the
claim and its competing explanations: bilateral hand wrenches for hand-load
allocation, shaft measurements for deformation, or activation observations for
an activation hypothesis. Not every question requires the same sensor list;
EMG does not directly measure muscle force. The full project protocol requests
multiple synchronized modalities because its joint claims cross these boundaries.
Chapters 25 and 26 connect measurement sufficiency to identifiability and design.

**Model Result:** The pinned release reports bounded interaction and
force-generated-couple findings in specified planar and reduced spatial
branches. It also includes qualified short-horizon articulated cases, while
broader anatomical transport remains unresolved. “Articulated” is not one
universal pass/fail label: capability, duration, contact law, and calibration
must accompany it. In its finite-base work-matching experiment, numerical gates
pass for 576 trajectories but no fixed-versus-coupled comparison cell meets the
registered total-work match. Consequently, that experiment identifies no delivery
benefit; numerical success cannot supply a missing matched comparison.

**Human Evidence:** The reviewed release has no qualifying controlled participant
deposit for its complete bilateral-wrench protocol. That is an evidence boundary
for this project and revision, not a claim that no relevant measurements exist
anywhere. Published kinematics or net kinetics support narrower questions.

For example, McNally and McPhee's six-degree-of-freedom model combines pelvis motion,
a second shoulder coordinate, flexible-club dynamics, and an impact/flight
objective [@mcnally2018]. Its optimization constrains some joint timings together
and assumes candidate center-face impacts. The authors report a
torso-before-pelvis timing result and grip-kinematic discrepancies, discussing
rigid-torso limitations. This is a useful example of testing a richer model against selected
observations, not evidence that its optimum identifies a golfer's muscle control.

**Practical Interpretation:** Ask for the smallest model that can answer today's
question and a comparison that can expose a consequential simplification. One
successful extension supplies bounded support, not proof against every omitted
mechanism.

### Why No Single Model Is “the Model”

Every model answers a question by omitting something. A double pendulum isolates
linked inertia. A two-hand constraint model exposes force allocation. A flexible
shaft adds stored energy and phase. A whole-body spatial model adds moving base
and ground interaction. A musculoskeletal model asks about candidate muscle
allocations. None supersedes all earlier models; each changes the balance between
interpretability, fidelity, and identifiability.

The ladder works when observables and interventions remain aligned across rungs.
If every model uses a different definition of transfer, comparison is impossible.
This project carries forward available hand-wrench, swing-normal-couple,
interface-power, work, club-state, closure, and intervention records with their
capability limits. None may be silently filled from a different model.

The following families organize modeling questions. They are not a claim that
every listed capability has been executed or validated together in one release.

### Rung Zero: Algebra and Geometry

Before integrating motion, test wrench arithmetic, sign conventions, moment-arm
dependencies, and coordinate transforms. Symbolic or static examples should
recover known limits exactly. This rung catches errors that a complex animation
can conceal.

It also states propositions clearly: collapsing hand separation collapses a pure
differential couple; a consistent reference-point transform preserves wrench
power; equal-and-opposite contacts can have zero net force and nonzero moment.
These are mechanics identities, not human findings.

### Rung One: The Planar Double Pendulum

The fixed-base two-link model tests interaction dynamics, carried motion,
relative release, and torque timing. Its small state permits dense parameter
sweeps, analytic checks, and transparent pointwise decompositions. It cannot
represent bilateral hands, spatial axes, ground contact, or shaft deformation.

A result promoted from this rung should be qualitative and mechanism-focused.
Exact speed gains or optimal milliseconds are provisional. Negative controls
and sensitivity maps determine which signs or orderings are stable enough to
carry upward.

### Rung Two: Two Hands and a Moving Base

Add separated contact points and declare either prescribed or dynamic proximal
motion. An algebraic two-hand representation can display common and differential
force modes, but geometry alone does not determine their forces. A forward
contact model needs the constitutive law, state, drivers, and constraints that
close its dynamics. A finite-mass dynamic base allows club-to-base reaction to
change base motion; a prescribed base instead requires whatever external
actuation enforces its trace. Contact remains idealized and anatomy generalized.

This rung asks whether the mechanism survives when the very feature it concerns
—two hands—is represented explicitly. It also exposes a possible inverse
ambiguity: the same club wrench can admit different hand allocations. Additional
measurements or constitutive restrictions can reduce that set; its dimension and
feasible extent are not fixed solely by having two contacts.

### Rung Three: Flexible Club

Add one or more shaft modes, damping, and calibrated boundary coupling. Repeat
the same counterfactuals while including modal state and energy. This rung asks
whether rigid-club conclusions were artifacts of omitting deformation and
whether negative coupling interacts with shaft return.

Modal convergence and independent beam checks matter. A single arbitrary spring
can generate an attractive delay without representing a club. Parameters should
come from measured or explicitly synthetic sources and remain qualified.

### Rung Four: Spatial Whole-Body Dynamics

Add three-dimensional pelvis, trunk, shoulder/arm, hand, and club motion with
ground contact. Spatial frames permit out-of-plane moments and full wrenches.
The number of parameters and controls grows sharply, so identifiability becomes
a central result rather than an inconvenience.

Independent implementations are valuable here, provided the physical problem
and compared outputs are matched. Similar trajectories alone can hide incorrect
load or power bookkeeping. Conversely, different contact laws need not predict
identical reactions: first decide whether the test concerns implementation
agreement or sensitivity to physical assumptions. One implementation is not
automatically wrong, but it leaves that replication question open.

### Rung Five: Biological Allocation

A musculoskeletal or activation-aware model proposes how generalized loads might
be shared among muscles and passive tissues. It can study co-contraction,
stiffness, and internal load, but it needs EMG, strength, anatomy, and optimization
assumptions. Multiple allocations usually fit the same motion.

This rung should not retroactively turn earlier generalized arm and wrist drivers
into named muscles. Instead it tests candidate mappings and reports their
nonuniqueness. Scapular action, in particular, requires adequate kinematics and
measurement-aware shoulder-girdle representation.

### Promotion and Demotion Rules

A claim earns support in an additional model only for the registered outputs,
interventions, and domain that were tested. Keep four different outcomes apart:
a failed closure check prevents numerical qualification; a resolved adverse
prediction can contradict the registered claim; insufficient measurements leave
it inconclusive; an unrun comparison remains untested. Changing a constitutive
law and reversing an effect demonstrates sensitivity to that assumption, not
automatically a bug or a contradiction of the original conditional statement.

Demotion is not failure of the project. It locates a boundary: “this effect is
specific to a fixed-base rigid planar model” is scientifically useful. The
reader can then see what remains established, what is model-conditional, and
what human evidence still owes.

### Cross-Rung Tables and Figures

For each mechanism, a comparison table should list degrees of freedom, contact
model, shaft model, controls, identified parameters, pass/fail gates, and common
outcomes. Figures should overlay normalized time histories with consistent
signs, not juxtapose unrelated axes. Differences in magnitude should remain
visible rather than normalized away when magnitude is the question.

Machine-readable manifests make this comparison reproducible. Each row links to
input, output, code commit, and generated figure. Reviewers can rerun one rung or
replace it with an independent implementation without adopting the whole
software ecosystem.

### Deciding When Complexity Is Worth It

Add a degree of freedom or state when it changes a target observable, explains a
structured residual, enables a discriminating experiment, or removes an
unacceptable assumption. Do not add complexity merely for visual realism.
Weakly constrained flexibility can absorb residuals and weaken discrimination
among explanations. It does not literally allow every possible observation;
the question is which alternatives the chosen data and test can distinguish.

The final modeling product should therefore remain modular: a transparent core,
optional higher-fidelity rungs, shared contracts, and explicit qualification.
That architecture invites criticism and extension as an open resource rather
than presenting one branded engine as final authority.

### Reader Lab: Write a Promotion Matrix

Choose one claim, such as a late negative swing-normal contact couple. Across
rows list algebraic geometry, planar double pendulum, two-hand moving base,
flexible shaft, spatial whole-body, and biological allocation. Across columns
list sign, onset, duration, magnitude, work, outcome effect, negative controls,
uncertainty, and human evidence. Populate every cell with result, not applicable,
or unresolved.

The matrix makes a common error obvious: a claim may be well verified in early
rungs but unresolved in humans. It also reveals where complexity changes the
result. Link each cell to machine-readable evidence and tests.

Define comparison criteria before looking at outcomes. A chosen rule might
require the sign in 95 percent of a declared ensemble, with geometry controls
passing, while permitting bounded changes in magnitude. That percentage is a
decision rule about a specified sample and weighting, not a universal probability
or confidence guarantee. Three positive results among four scenarios give 75%
with equal weights, but 30% with weights $(0.1,0.1,0.1,0.7)$ when the last result
is negative. Neither weighting becomes a golfer population without evidence.

Even under independent sampling from a specified Bernoulli population, 95
successes in 100 trials give an approximate 95% Wilson interval of
$[0.888,0.978]$ for its success probability, not proof that it is at least 0.95.
A deterministic parameter grid or correlated trajectories do not automatically
justify that binomial calculation. Declare scenario selection, dependence,
weights, adverse cases, and held-out checks. Keep statistical uncertainty
separate from untested model discrepancy.

### Independent Extension

Invite a second implementation to reproduce one rung using the published
contracts. If it disagrees, preserve both outputs and reconcile specification,
frames, and numerics. The goal is not to defend an engine. It is to discover
which physical conclusion survives independent expression.

A modular open resource makes such extension inexpensive. Shared schemas and
benchmarks let a contributor add a contact or anatomical rung without rewriting
the manuscript's conceptual core.

### A Claim Can Live at More Than One Rung

The identity that rigid-body wrench power is reference-point invariant requires
paired transport of moment and velocity for the same physical port motion.
The finding that a particular
negative-couple interval appears belongs to specific model rungs. The hypothesis
that golfers use it belongs to the human-evidence rung. Separating them prevents
a human null result from invalidating an identity or a verified identity from
being offered as human validation.

Each public statement should therefore carry rung and status. Readers can see
which parts are durable foundations and which remain contingent. New evidence
updates the appropriate layer without rewriting the entire framework.

### Completion Is a Maintained Ladder

A release can be complete as an audited record while leaving proposed branches
untested. Each included result needs a specification, executed verification,
available observables, limitations, and the next discriminating test; proposed
extensions need explicit untested status. Documentation completeness is neither
completion of every experiment nor validation of maximal anatomical detail.

Maintaining simple benchmarks alongside rich models prevents regression and
keeps the project teachable. The lay book, technical monograph, simulator, and
evidence register should all reference the same ladder identifiers.

## Where the Picture Breaks

The map analogy suggests clean nested scales. Model families are not always
nested; a spatial engine may use different contact or damping laws rather than
simply adding detail. Common observables and negative controls are needed to
compare them fairly.

More agreement also does not guarantee truth if all tiers share a wrong premise.
Independent measurement remains decisive.
